overview: The Cuman-Kipchak confederation linked regional steppe powers without one centralized state. This card covers the atlas’s 1100-1200 confederation and 1200-1279 Cuman Khanates records. The earlier outline extends into Mongolia, beyond the core range supported here, and is not a verified border. Neither cutoff marks the disappearance of the people. Mongol conquest broke up independent power in the 1230s.

periods.title: Expansion and regional alliances
periods.summary: Cuman-Kipchak groupings became powerful neighbours, allies and rivals of surrounding kingdoms.

periods.title: Conquest and westward migration
periods.summary: Mongol expansion disrupted steppe power; Cuman groups sought refuge and alliances farther west.

periods.title: Communities under new rulers
periods.summary: Cuman communities continued in Hungary and the Mongol-ruled steppe; the surviving language manuscript belongs to this later world.

items.text: The wider confederation contained several regional groupings: western Cumans, Central Asian Kipchak-Qangli and western Siberian Kipchaks. Their leaders could make different alliances. A single coloured map region should not suggest one capital issuing orders to every camp.

Family connections carried political weight. The Georgian king David was the son-in-law of the Cuman leader Otrok, whose followers sought refuge in Georgia after campaigns by Vladimir Monomakh. Cuman soldiers helped the Georgian crown become a stronger regional power.

Trade routes linked Khwarazm, Volga Bulgaria, Rus’ lands and Black Sea markets. Cuman leaders and communities could profit from exchange or tribute, while raiding and captive-taking also brought wealth at others’ expense. Peaceful business and warfare were closely entangled.

Mongol pressure pushed some Cuman groups west. Khan Kuthen sought asylum in Hungary in 1239, where King Bela IV wanted military allies. Suspicion and violence led to Kuthen’s killing and a Cuman departure; groups later returned. Migration was a difficult negotiation over safety, land and power.

Herding was central to steppe livelihoods, but life varied across the enormous region. Some communities appear to have made winter camps more permanent and added cultivation. Keeping animals required practical knowledge of pasture and seasons, rather than simply wandering wherever the horses wished.

External writers describe felt homes that could travel, and both texts and archaeology attest wagons. Yet chronicles also name Cuman strongholds such as Sharukan and Sugrov. Portable dwellings, settled places and political centres could coexist; owning a wagon did not make someone homeless.

Food accounts need their dates attached. In the fourteenth century, after Mongol conquest, Ibn Battuta described Kipchak-region meals of millet soup with meat and fermented mare’s milk. It is a vivid later snapshot, not proof that every earlier Cuman household ate the same things.

A stone woman from Stadnytsya, dated around the twelfth or thirteenth century, wears a long caftan, a tall hat, earrings and a necklace. Her belt carries a pouch. The sculpture preserves details of clothing and accessories that normally decay much faster than stone.

Behind that statue’s head are hornlike decorations made as fabric-covered rolls of felt. They are part of her headgear, not animal horns growing from her head! Her hands hold a vessel. The museum does not know why someone later removed the face’s details.

At the Chungul Kurgan in southern Ukraine, a rich medieval burial was inserted into an older Bronze Age mound. Researchers date this burial to the early thirteenth century. Its imported luxury objects reveal far-reaching contacts, though they do not securely identify the deceased by name.

Clothing from that burial was assembled from different silks, gold decoration and reused textiles; two preserved caftans had marten-fur linings. Researchers interpret the garments as combining a riding coat’s familiar form with the prestigious decoration of neighbouring courts. Even a magnificent coat could contain carefully reused cloth.

Cuman stone figures show both women and men, sometimes with weapons or armour, holding vessels in front of their bodies. The Neues Museum interprets these cups as signs of the dead joining a shared drink. That reading connects sculpture with remembrance and communal ritual.

sections.title: Language and a puzzle to try

items.text: The Codex Cumanicus survives in Venice as a fourteenth-century manuscript. Its vocabulary records Cuman alongside Latin and Persian, while another section contains grammar, word lists and Christian religious texts. It shows people working across languages in the post-conquest Black Sea and lower Volga world.

Here is a later Cuman riddle in modern scholarly transcription of its Latin-script text: “Ak küyməniŋ avzu yox. Ol, yumurtka.” It means: “A white tent has no mouth. It’s an egg.” The comparison turns an ordinary shell into a tiny house with no entrance.

This was also a tool for language learning: the compilers arranged word lists and grammatical forms, and translated texts for religious services. It documents a particular multilingual teaching effort, rather than a school system attended by all Cuman children.

The surviving codex is about 20 by 14 centimetres and has 82 paper leaves. Its opening carries an older date, 1303, but the manuscript was copied and expanded; the Veneto catalogue dates the copy to 1330. A date at a book’s beginning is not automatically every page’s birthday.

At the later medieval Cuman village of Orgondaszentmiklos in Hungary, excavators found house plots with bases interpreted as yurts nearby. Families could use buildings and tentlike structures together. This evidence belongs to settled descendants in Hungary, not automatically to the earlier Black Sea camps.

Animal bones from that village carry traces of butchery and dogs’ teeth, suggesting food refuse lay where dogs could reach it. A horse’s pelvic injury with signs of healing also suggests people kept it alive after a serious accident. The bones do not reveal a specific treatment.

ending.text: Mongol conquest in the 1230s ended independent Cuman-Kipchak power across much of the steppe. Communities continued under Mongol rule and in Hungary and elsewhere, contributing to later societies.
